title: Krishna Reappears Among the Gopis
story:
For a long while the gopis had searched the forest, and their grief had seemed to have no end. Krishna had vanished — twice now — and the second vanishing had taken from them even the thin comfort of hoping that searching would bring him back. Then, when they had nearly stopped looking, he was simply there before them: smiling, his face bright and open as a lotus.

The verses say only that he appeared. One moment the grove held nothing but their own sorrow; the next he stood among them, and the sorrow was not reasoned away — it left them all at once. They rose as if life itself had come back into their bodies. Their eyes, a moment before downcast and searching, bloomed open with joy.

And because no two of them loved him in the same way, no two of them received him in the same way. One took his hand in her two folded palms and held it, as you would hold something too precious to let fall. One, slender and quick, bent and lifted from him the betel he had been chewing, and kept it cupped in her own palms like a gift she would not share. Another knit her brows at him, flushed with an anger that was really love, silently reproaching him for having left her to such grief. Another did not blink at all, drinking in his face as if afraid that the moment she closed her eyes he would be gone again. And one more did not look with her eyes; she gathered him into her heart through the narrow opening of her closed lids, and kept him there, where he could not leave.

The verses linger on this, because it is the whole meaning of the scene: all of them, every one, overjoyed at the sight of him, their grief of separation washed clean. They pressed around him, and he stood among them.

Then he led them away from the place of their grief to the bright sandbank of the Yamuna. It was autumn, and the moon was full; its light lay on the water and the sand like something poured out, and the verses say that light drove away the darkness of all that was wrong. There, in that light, the ache in their hearts was dispelled, and their longings came to rest — the way, the verses say, the ancient scriptures themselves come to rest when they have carried a person all the way home.

He sat down among them. He was the master of every master of yoga, and yet the seat he accepted was the one they had already prepared for him — not any throne, but the seat they had made for him inside their own hearts. They welcomed him with smiles, with sidelong glances, with the small glad play of their brows: the language of people who have been given back what they thought was lost.

There is no rebuke in the scene, and no explanation. Krishna does not say why he had vanished, and the gopis do not ask. Whatever they needed to hear, they would hear soon enough. For this one moment, the answer was simply that he had come back.
reflection: The scene is made of small, individual gestures — a hand held, a bit of betel kept, an unblinking gaze — because the verses want the reunion to be felt one gopi at a time and then all at once. Here grief is not dispelled by argument but by presence.
next_story_tease: But the gopis still carried a question they needed to ask him.
hero_scene: Krishna reappearing with a smiling lotus-bright face among the grieving gopis on the moonlit sandbank of the Yamuna, each gopi receiving him in her own way — one holding his hand in folded palms, one cupping the betel he had chewed, one gazing at him with unblinking eyes.
